tooltips.name: RotorThrust
tooltips.title: Thrust
tooltips.meaning: Thrust is the pushing or pulling force a propeller or rotor produces.
tooltips.effect: In straight, level flight, forward thrust greater than drag (air resistance) lets the aircraft speed up. Extra thrust can also help it climb.
tooltips.example: If thrust is 1,200 N and drag is 1,000 N, the forward force left over is 200 N.
tooltips.units: Force units consistent with the solver inputs: N in SI or lbf with slug-ft-s inputs.

tooltips.name: RotorPower
tooltips.title: Power
tooltips.meaning: Power is how quickly the engine or motor supplies energy to turn the propeller.
tooltips.effect: More available power can support more thrust, but the propeller and flight speed determine how much. Power is not the same as thrust.
tooltips.example: In consistent SI inputs, 20,000 means 20,000 watts, not 20 kilowatts.
tooltips.units: W with kg-m-s inputs; ft-lbf/s with slug-ft-s inputs, not horsepower.

tooltips.name: RotorTorque
tooltips.title: Torque
tooltips.meaning: Torque is the twisting force the motor applies to the propeller shaft.
tooltips.effect: The motor and shaft must withstand it. Torque multiplied by turning speed gives shaft power.
tooltips.example: A longer spanner turns a stiff nut more easily: it gives more torque.
tooltips.units: N-m with SI inputs; ft-lbf with slug-ft-s inputs.

tooltips.name: RotorRPM
tooltips.title: Propeller speed
tooltips.meaning: RPM is how many full turns the propeller makes in one minute.
tooltips.effect: Changing RPM changes blade airflow, thrust, power demand and noise. Faster is not automatically more efficient.
tooltips.example: 2,400 RPM means 40 complete turns every second.

tooltips.name: RotorDiameter
tooltips.title: Rotor diameter
tooltips.meaning: The diameter is the distance across the full circle swept by the blade tips.
tooltips.effect: A larger disk can move more air, but needs ground clearance and a suitable motor and blade design.
tooltips.example: A 2 m diameter gives a 1 m distance from the centre to a blade tip.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: RotorHubDiameter
tooltips.title: Hub diameter
tooltips.meaning: The hub is the centre of the rotor disk where the blade roots attach.
tooltips.effect: This setting describes the central region rather than the blade-tip size. An oversized hub leaves less working disk area.
tooltips.example: Do not enter the full propeller diameter in the hub box.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: AutoHubDiaFlag
tooltips.title: Automatic hub size
tooltips.meaning: This takes the hub diameter from the propeller shape instead of a manually entered value.
tooltips.effect: It keeps the rotor disk setup linked to the propeller geometry.
tooltips.example: Use Auto after changing the blade-root shape so you do not keep an old hub size.

tooltips.name: RotorCT
tooltips.title: Thrust coefficient
tooltips.meaning: C_T describes thrust relative to air density, turning speed and propeller diameter.
tooltips.effect: At the same density, RPM and diameter, a larger C_T means more thrust. It is not thrust in newtons.
tooltips.example: Use coefficients measured or predicted for your propeller and operating condition.

tooltips.name: RotorCP
tooltips.title: Power coefficient
tooltips.meaning: C_P describes shaft power relative to air density, turning speed and propeller diameter.
tooltips.effect: At the same density, RPM and diameter, a larger C_P means the propeller needs more shaft power.
tooltips.example: Do not enter engine horsepower in a C_P box.

tooltips.name: RotorCQ
tooltips.title: Torque coefficient
tooltips.meaning: C_Q describes shaft torque relative to density, turning speed and propeller diameter.
tooltips.effect: It helps relate propeller loading to the torque required from the motor.
tooltips.example: Compare C_Q values only when the same coefficient convention is used.

tooltips.name: RotorJ
tooltips.title: Advance ratio
tooltips.meaning: Advance ratio compares forward airspeed with how fast the propeller turns and how large it is.
tooltips.effect: It identifies the operating point on a propeller performance chart.
tooltips.example: At zero forward speed J is zero, even when the propeller is turning.

tooltips.name: RotorEta
tooltips.title: Propeller efficiency
tooltips.meaning: Efficiency is useful forward thrust power divided by the shaft power supplied.
tooltips.effect: A more efficient propeller wastes less of the supplied power at that flight condition.
tooltips.example: 0.80 means 80 percent in forward flight. This efficiency measure is not useful for static thrust.

tooltips.name: TotalSpan
tooltips.title: Whole-wing span
tooltips.meaning: Span measures how far the wing extends from root to tip, including its mirrored side when symmetry is on.
tooltips.effect: At the same lift and speed, a greater span generally reduces the drag caused by producing lift, but adds structural demands.
tooltips.example: With a single mirrored section, 5 units on each side gives 10 units total.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: TotalProjectedSpan
tooltips.title: Projected wing span
tooltips.meaning: This is the wing width measured in a top view, ignoring its upward or downward tilt.
tooltips.effect: An angled wing has less top-view width than the same wing laid flat.
tooltips.example: Use this to compare the top-view sizes of a flat wing and a wing with dihedral.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: TotalArea
tooltips.title: Whole-wing area
tooltips.meaning: Wing area measures the size of the wing using its front-to-back chords and section widths. It includes the mirrored side when symmetry is on.
tooltips.effect: For the same weight and maximum lift coefficient, more area lowers the estimated stall speed. Weight and drag may also change.
tooltips.example: A simple rectangular wing 10 m wide and 1.5 m deep has 15 square metres of area.

tooltips.name: TotalChord
tooltips.title: Average wing chord
tooltips.meaning: Chord is the front-to-back length of a wing. This value averages the section average chords.
tooltips.effect: A greater chord at the same span increases wing area. On a multi-section wing, this simple average is not necessarily area divided by span.
tooltips.example: A rectangular wing with 1.5 m chords has a 1.5 m average chord.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: TotalAR
tooltips.title: Whole-wing aspect ratio
tooltips.meaning: Aspect ratio describes how long and narrow the wing is: span squared divided by area.
tooltips.effect: Higher aspect ratio generally reduces lift-related drag, but does not guarantee lower total drag or a lighter wing.
tooltips.example: A 10 m span and 20 square metres of area give an aspect ratio of 5.

tooltips.name: MAC
tooltips.title: Mean aerodynamic chord
tooltips.meaning: MAC is a representative wing chord used to describe aerodynamic balance and pitching moments.
tooltips.effect: It provides a useful length for comparing centre-of-gravity positions, especially on tapered wings.
tooltips.example: A CG shift of 0.1 m is 10 percent of MAC when MAC is 1 m.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: CurvedArea
tooltips.title: Area with curved edges
tooltips.meaning: This measures wing area while accounting for curved leading and trailing edges.
tooltips.effect: It can differ from the straight-edged section planform area and change the chosen reference area for analysis.
tooltips.example: A curved wingtip can change this area without changing the section corner points.

tooltips.name: RelativeDihedralFlag
tooltips.title: Relative dihedral
tooltips.meaning: Choose whether section dihedral is measured from the previous section or from the common reference plane.
tooltips.effect: This changes how section angles combine along a multi-section wing.
tooltips.example: Check the complete wing after changing the mode; the same entered number can describe a different final angle.

tooltips.name: RelativeTwistFlag
tooltips.title: Relative twist
tooltips.meaning: Choose whether section twist is added to the previous section or measured from the common reference orientation.
tooltips.effect: This changes how section angles combine along a multi-section wing.
tooltips.example: Check the complete wing after changing the mode; the same entered number can describe a different final angle.

tooltips.name: CorrectAirfoilthicknessFlag
tooltips.title: Airfoil thickness correction
tooltips.meaning: This adjusts airfoil thickness when sections are rotated to match dihedral.
tooltips.effect: It keeps the intended section thickness under that rotation. Near a 90-degree dihedral break the correction can become very large.
tooltips.example: Make a vertical fin by rotating the whole wing on XForm, not by forcing a section to 90-degree dihedral.

tooltips.name: Span
tooltips.title: Section span
tooltips.meaning: The width of this one wing section, from its inner edge to its outer edge.
tooltips.effect: Increasing it extends this section; the wing totals also depend on the other sections and symmetry.
tooltips.example: On a mirrored, single-section wing, a section span of 5 gives a total span of 10.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: ProjectedSpan
tooltips.title: Projected section span
tooltips.meaning: This section's width as measured from directly above.
tooltips.effect: Tilting the section upward reduces its top-view width.
tooltips.example: Compare it with section span after adding dihedral.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Area
tooltips.title: Section wing area
tooltips.meaning: The size of this section's flat wing outline, not the whole mirrored wing.
tooltips.effect: More section area can reduce wing loading, but mass and aerodynamic behaviour still need analysis.
tooltips.example: For a rectangular section, area equals section span times chord.

tooltips.name: Aspect
tooltips.title: Section aspect ratio
tooltips.meaning: The section span squared divided by its planform area.
tooltips.effect: This sets the section's long-and-narrow shape; it is not necessarily the whole-wing aspect ratio.
tooltips.example: A section 5 m wide and 1 m deep has aspect ratio 5.

tooltips.name: Root_Chord
tooltips.title: Section root chord
tooltips.meaning: The front-to-back wing length at this section's inner end.
tooltips.effect: Changing it changes area and taper and can affect adjacent sections.
tooltips.example: The first section's root chord is normally the chord nearest the fuselage.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Tip_Chord
tooltips.title: Section tip chord
tooltips.meaning: The front-to-back wing length at this section's outer end.
tooltips.effect: Reducing it makes this section more tapered; stall behaviour also depends on the airfoil and twist.
tooltips.example: A 1 m tip chord with a 2 m root chord gives a taper ratio of 0.5.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Avg_Chord
tooltips.title: Section average chord
tooltips.meaning: The average front-to-back length of this wing section.
tooltips.effect: For a straight-edged section, it is the average of the root and tip chords.
tooltips.example: A 2 m root chord and 1 m tip chord average to 1.5 m.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Taper
tooltips.title: Taper ratio
tooltips.meaning: Tip chord divided by root chord: how much the wing narrows toward this section's outer end.
tooltips.effect: Lower values make a more pointed section; they do not automatically give safer stalling or better performance.
tooltips.example: 1 means equal chords; 0.5 means the tip is half as deep as the root.

tooltips.name: Sweep
tooltips.title: Wing sweep
tooltips.meaning: The backward or forward angle of this section at the selected chord location.
tooltips.effect: Sweep changes where area lies along the aircraft and can help at high speed, but has low-speed trade-offs.
tooltips.example: 0 degrees is unswept at the selected measurement line.

tooltips.name: Sec_Sweep
tooltips.title: Secondary sweep
tooltips.meaning: The sweep measured at a second front-to-back position on the chord.
tooltips.effect: It helps define the same section geometry using another measurement line.
tooltips.example: Leading-edge sweep and trailing-edge sweep can differ on a tapered wing.

tooltips.name: Sweep_Location
tooltips.title: Sweep measurement line
tooltips.meaning: Where along the chord the main sweep angle is measured.
tooltips.effect: Changing the measurement line changes what the sweep number describes.
tooltips.example: 0 means leading edge; 0.25 means quarter-chord; 1 means trailing edge.

tooltips.name: Sec_Sweep_Location
tooltips.title: Secondary sweep line
tooltips.meaning: Where along the chord the secondary sweep angle is measured.
tooltips.effect: It must describe a different chordwise line from the main sweep location.
tooltips.example: Use 1 for trailing-edge sweep if the main location is 0.

tooltips.name: Dihedral
tooltips.title: Dihedral
tooltips.meaning: The upward or downward tilt of a wing section as seen from the front.
tooltips.effect: It affects how the aircraft responds to sideways airflow. Positive dihedral often helps roll stability, but does not guarantee self-levelling.
tooltips.example: A shallow V shape seen head-on has positive dihedral.

tooltips.name: Twist
tooltips.title: Wing twist
tooltips.meaning: The rotation applied to the airfoil at this section station.
tooltips.effect: It changes local angle of attack. A lower tip angle can help the root stall first, depending on the complete wing.
tooltips.example: A tip set 2 degrees lower than the root is called 2 degrees of washout.

tooltips.name: Twist_Location
tooltips.title: Twist rotation point
tooltips.meaning: The front-to-back point on the chord about which the airfoil is twisted.
tooltips.effect: It changes which part of the airfoil stays in place while its angle changes.
tooltips.example: 0.25 places the rotation point one quarter of the way behind the leading edge.

tooltips.name: Length
tooltips.title: Fuselage length
tooltips.meaning: The nose-to-tail length of this fuselage.
tooltips.effect: A longer fuselage offers more internal space and changes surface area and tail placement. It does not set the real aircraft mass automatically.
tooltips.example: If your model uses metres, 7 means a 7 m body.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Length
tooltips.title: Pod length
tooltips.meaning: The end-to-end length of this streamlined pod.
tooltips.effect: Changing it changes the pod size and its surface area; drag must be evaluated at a flight condition.
tooltips.example: Use a pod to sketch a tank or equipment fairing.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: FineRatio
tooltips.title: Pod fineness ratio
tooltips.meaning: Here this is pod length divided by its greatest radius, not its diameter.
tooltips.effect: For a fixed length, a larger value makes the pod slimmer.
tooltips.example: Length 10 and ratio 5 give a largest radius of 2.

tooltips.name: Width
tooltips.title: Cross-section width
tooltips.meaning: The side-to-side width of this slice through the body.
tooltips.effect: It changes the local body shape and available internal space.
tooltips.example: Make the middle sections wide for payload and the nose sections narrow.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Height
tooltips.title: Cross-section height
tooltips.meaning: The top-to-bottom height of this slice through the body.
tooltips.effect: It changes local body depth; it is not the aircraft's height above the ground.
tooltips.example: A wide, low section makes a flattened body shape.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Area
tooltips.title: Cross-section area
tooltips.meaning: The area enclosed by this section curve, not wing planform area.
tooltips.effect: It measures the size of this slice and helps define the body shape.
tooltips.example: For a circular section, a larger radius gives a larger enclosed area.

tooltips.name: HWRatio
tooltips.title: Section height-to-width ratio
tooltips.meaning: Cross-section height divided by cross-section width.
tooltips.effect: Values greater than 1 make the section taller than it is wide.
tooltips.example: A 2 m height and 1 m width give a ratio of 2.

tooltips.name: Chord
tooltips.title: Airfoil chord
tooltips.meaning: The straight-line distance from the front of the airfoil to its back.
tooltips.effect: It sets the airfoil size. The thickness-to-chord ratio separately controls how thick it is.
tooltips.example: A 1 m chord with 0.12 thickness ratio has a maximum thickness of about 0.12 m.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: ThickChord
tooltips.title: Airfoil thickness ratio
tooltips.meaning: Maximum airfoil thickness divided by chord.
tooltips.effect: Thicker airfoils can provide more room for structure, but lift, drag and stall behaviour also depend on the complete airfoil shape.
tooltips.example: 0.12 means 12 percent of chord, not 12 length units.

tooltips.name: Camber
tooltips.title: Airfoil camber
tooltips.meaning: The bend of the airfoil's middle line, expressed as a fraction of chord.
tooltips.effect: Camber changes lift and pitching tendency; more camber does not guarantee less drag.
tooltips.example: 0.02 means maximum camber is 2 percent of chord.

tooltips.name: CamberLoc
tooltips.title: Camber location
tooltips.meaning: Where along the chord the maximum bend of the airfoil occurs.
tooltips.effect: Moving it changes the airfoil shape and its aerodynamic behaviour.
tooltips.example: 0.4 puts maximum camber 40 percent of the way back from the leading edge.

tooltips.name: Invert
tooltips.title: Invert airfoil
tooltips.meaning: Flip this airfoil section upside down.
tooltips.effect: It reverses the direction of its camber; it does not change the wing's position.
tooltips.example: An inverted cambered airfoil can be useful when exploring tail shapes.

tooltips.name: IdealCl
tooltips.title: Airfoil design lift coefficient
tooltips.meaning: A lift coefficient associated with the airfoil's designed camber.
tooltips.effect: It helps describe the airfoil design point; it is not a measured maximum lift coefficient.
tooltips.example: Do not use this value as CLmax in a stall-speed calculation.

tooltips.name: XLocPercent
tooltips.title: Lengthwise section position
tooltips.meaning: The front-to-back position of this body section, expressed as a fraction of fuselage length.
tooltips.effect: Moving sections changes the body outline without moving the whole component.
tooltips.example: 0.5 is half a fuselage length in the X direction.

tooltips.name: YLocPercent
tooltips.title: Sideways section position
tooltips.meaning: The left-to-right position of this body section, expressed as a fraction of fuselage length.
tooltips.effect: Moving sections changes the body outline without moving the whole component.
tooltips.example: 0.5 is half a fuselage length in the Y direction.

tooltips.name: ZLocPercent
tooltips.title: Vertical section position
tooltips.meaning: The up-and-down position of this body section, expressed as a fraction of fuselage length.
tooltips.effect: Moving sections changes the body outline without moving the whole component.
tooltips.example: 0.5 is half a fuselage length in the Z direction.

tooltips.name: X_Location
tooltips.title: X global position
tooltips.meaning: The component's lengthwise position in the whole-model coordinate system.
tooltips.effect: Changing it moves this component; it does not resize it.
tooltips.example: Move a tail further behind the wing.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: X_Rel_Location
tooltips.title: X relative position
tooltips.meaning: The component's lengthwise position relative to its parent in the chosen attachment frame.
tooltips.effect: Changing it moves this component; it does not resize it.
tooltips.example: Move a tail further behind the wing.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Y_Location
tooltips.title: Y global position
tooltips.meaning: The component's sideways position in the whole-model coordinate system.
tooltips.effect: Changing it moves this component; it does not resize it.
tooltips.example: Move a nacelle away from the centreline.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Y_Rel_Location
tooltips.title: Y relative position
tooltips.meaning: The component's sideways position relative to its parent in the chosen attachment frame.
tooltips.effect: Changing it moves this component; it does not resize it.
tooltips.example: Move a nacelle away from the centreline.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Z_Location
tooltips.title: Z global position
tooltips.meaning: The component's up or down position in the whole-model coordinate system.
tooltips.effect: Changing it moves this component; it does not resize it.
tooltips.example: Raise a wing above the fuselage.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Z_Rel_Location
tooltips.title: Z relative position
tooltips.meaning: The component's up or down position relative to its parent in the chosen attachment frame.
tooltips.effect: Changing it moves this component; it does not resize it.
tooltips.example: Raise a wing above the fuselage.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: X_Rotation
tooltips.title: X global rotation
tooltips.meaning: Turn this component about the lengthwise axis in the model frame.
tooltips.effect: This changes its orientation rather than its dimensions.
tooltips.example: Rotate a wing about X to explore a vertical fin; check symmetry.

tooltips.name: X_Rel_Rotation
tooltips.title: X relative rotation
tooltips.meaning: Turn this component about the lengthwise axis relative to its parent.
tooltips.effect: This changes its orientation rather than its dimensions.
tooltips.example: Rotate a wing about X to explore a vertical fin; check symmetry.

tooltips.name: Y_Rotation
tooltips.title: Y global rotation
tooltips.meaning: Turn this component about the side-to-side axis in the model frame.
tooltips.effect: This changes its orientation rather than its dimensions.
tooltips.example: Tilt a wing to change its installed angle.

tooltips.name: Y_Rel_Rotation
tooltips.title: Y relative rotation
tooltips.meaning: Turn this component about the side-to-side axis relative to its parent.
tooltips.effect: This changes its orientation rather than its dimensions.
tooltips.example: Tilt a wing to change its installed angle.

tooltips.name: Z_Rotation
tooltips.title: Z global rotation
tooltips.meaning: Turn this component about the vertical axis in the model frame.
tooltips.effect: This changes its orientation rather than its dimensions.
tooltips.example: Turn a component sideways in top view.

tooltips.name: Z_Rel_Rotation
tooltips.title: Z relative rotation
tooltips.meaning: Turn this component about the vertical axis relative to its parent.
tooltips.effect: This changes its orientation rather than its dimensions.
tooltips.example: Turn a component sideways in top view.

tooltips.name: Scale
tooltips.title: Component scale
tooltips.meaning: A multiplier applied to the component dimensions.
tooltips.effect: Scaling changes lengths, areas and volumes; check mass assumptions and analysis units afterwards.
tooltips.example: Doubling all lengths makes area four times larger and volume eight times larger.

tooltips.name: Origin
tooltips.title: Rotation origin
tooltips.meaning: The location used as the pivot when the component rotates.
tooltips.effect: A different pivot changes how the component moves when you adjust its orientation.
tooltips.example: A door rotates about a hinge, not necessarily about its centre.

tooltips.name: Sym_Planar_Flag
tooltips.title: Mirror symmetry
tooltips.meaning: Mirror this component across one or more coordinate planes.
tooltips.effect: A half-wing can become a complete pair. Mirroring a fin already on the centre plane can create overlapping geometry.
tooltips.example: Use XZ symmetry for left and right wings; normally turn it off for a single vertical fin.

tooltips.name: Tess_U
tooltips.title: Along-surface mesh detail
tooltips.meaning: The number of surface divisions in one direction.
tooltips.effect: More divisions can improve geometric resolution but increase memory use and analysis time. They do not improve the physical design.
tooltips.example: Increase detail gradually and compare results to check that they stop changing significantly.

tooltips.name: Tess_W
tooltips.title: Around-section mesh detail
tooltips.meaning: The number of surface divisions in the other direction.
tooltips.effect: More divisions can improve geometric resolution but increase memory use and analysis time. They do not improve the physical design.
tooltips.example: Increase detail gradually and compare results to check that they stop changing significantly.

tooltips.name: Density
tooltips.title: Material density
tooltips.meaning: How much mass fills one unit of volume in this component.
tooltips.effect: Higher material density increases computed mass for the same volume and may move the centre of gravity.
tooltips.example: A solid block and a hollow shell need different mass assumptions. This is not outside air density.
tooltips.units: Mass per model-length unit cubed; keep mass and length units consistent.

tooltips.name: Mass_Area
tooltips.title: Mass per surface area
tooltips.meaning: How much mass is assigned to each unit of surface area when shell mass is enabled.
tooltips.effect: It estimates thin-skin mass without treating the whole enclosed volume as solid.
tooltips.example: A 3 square metre skin at 2 kg per square metre contributes 6 kg.

tooltips.name: Shell_Flag
tooltips.title: Use shell mass
tooltips.meaning: Include area-based mass for this component's skin.
tooltips.effect: Use it for thin surfaces. Check the volume-density setting too so you do not unintentionally count mass twice.
tooltips.example: A hollow fuselage shell should not be modelled as a solid block of aluminium.

tooltips.name: Mass_Prior
tooltips.title: Overlap mass priority
tooltips.meaning: Which component takes priority when volume-based mass regions overlap.
tooltips.effect: The highest priority wins in overlapping regions, so the selected densities matter.
tooltips.example: Check the mass result when a wing passes through the fuselage.

tooltips.name: PointMass
tooltips.title: Added point mass
tooltips.meaning: Mass concentrated at one location instead of spread through a volume.
tooltips.effect: It contributes to total mass and balance without needing a detailed solid model.
tooltips.example: Represent a battery with its mass and its actual position.

tooltips.name: CGx
tooltips.title: Point-mass X position
tooltips.meaning: The X coordinate used to locate this mass contribution.
tooltips.effect: Moving a mass changes aircraft balance and rotational inertia.
tooltips.example: A heavy battery moved rearward shifts the overall centre of gravity rearward.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: CGy
tooltips.title: Point-mass Y position
tooltips.meaning: The Y coordinate used to locate this mass contribution.
tooltips.effect: Moving a mass changes aircraft balance and rotational inertia.
tooltips.example: A heavy battery moved rearward shifts the overall centre of gravity rearward.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: CGz
tooltips.title: Point-mass Z position
tooltips.meaning: The Z coordinate used to locate this mass contribution.
tooltips.effect: Moving a mass changes aircraft balance and rotational inertia.
tooltips.example: A heavy battery moved rearward shifts the overall centre of gravity rearward.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: NumMassSlices
tooltips.title: Mass calculation slices
tooltips.meaning: How many slices are used to approximate volume-based mass properties.
tooltips.effect: More slices can improve resolution at the cost of calculation time. This is not an aircraft design dimension.
tooltips.example: Compare two slice counts and check whether the computed mass and CG settle down.

tooltips.name: NumMassSlice
tooltips.title: Mass calculation slices
tooltips.meaning: How many slices are used to approximate volume-based mass properties.
tooltips.effect: More slices can improve resolution at the cost of calculation time. This is not an aircraft design dimension.
tooltips.example: Compare two slice counts and check whether the computed mass and CG settle down.

tooltips.name: DrawCgFlag
tooltips.title: Show centre of gravity
tooltips.meaning: Display the calculated balance point in the 3D view.
tooltips.effect: It helps you compare the mass balance point with the wing and tail positions.
tooltips.example: Recompute mass properties after moving a heavy component.

tooltips.name: Diameter
tooltips.title: Propeller diameter
tooltips.meaning: The distance across the circle swept by the propeller blade tips.
tooltips.effect: A larger diameter sweeps more air but also changes power demand, tip speed and clearance.
tooltips.example: Check that the blade tips would clear the ground and fuselage.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: NumBlade
tooltips.title: Number of blades
tooltips.meaning: How many blades are on this propeller.
tooltips.effect: Extra blades can absorb more power within a limited diameter, but do not multiply thrust by blade count alone.
tooltips.example: A three-blade propeller is not automatically 50 percent stronger than a two-blade one.

tooltips.name: Beta34
tooltips.title: Blade pitch at 75 percent radius
tooltips.meaning: The blade angle measured three quarters of the way from the hub to the tip.
tooltips.effect: Pitch changes the blade's angle to its local airflow and therefore thrust and power demand.
tooltips.example: A suitable takeoff pitch may differ from a suitable cruise pitch.

tooltips.name: Feather
tooltips.title: Blade feather angle
tooltips.meaning: An overall pitch rotation applied to the propeller blade.
tooltips.effect: It changes blade loading; it is different from turning the whole propeller around its shaft.
tooltips.example: Feathering a stopped propeller can reduce its drag, depending on blade position.

tooltips.name: Precone
tooltips.title: Blade precone
tooltips.meaning: The built-in tilt of blades out of the rotor plane.
tooltips.effect: It changes the blade-tip path and rotor geometry.
tooltips.example: Seen from the side, a preconed rotor resembles a shallow cone.

tooltips.name: ReverseFlag
tooltips.title: Reverse rotation direction
tooltips.meaning: Choose the opposite direction of propeller rotation.
tooltips.effect: The geometry and solver setup must agree about which way the blades turn.
tooltips.example: A counter-rotating pair needs opposite rotation directions.

tooltips.name: Chord
tooltips.title: Blade chord / radius
tooltips.meaning: The mean blade chord divided by propeller radius, not a length in metres.
tooltips.effect: This ratio describes relative blade width; it is not a direct thrust setting.
tooltips.example: A mean chord ratio of 0.2 on a 1 m radius corresponds to a 0.2 m mean chord.

tooltips.name: Solidity
tooltips.title: Blade solidity
tooltips.meaning: How much of the rotor disk is occupied by blade planform area.
tooltips.effect: A larger value means more blade area relative to disk area and can change power absorption.
tooltips.example: Adding blades or making them wider increases solidity.

tooltips.name: PropMode
tooltips.title: Propeller display mode
tooltips.meaning: Represent this propeller with blades, a disk, or both.
tooltips.effect: This controls the geometric representation, not the engine power.
tooltips.example: A disk is a simplified view of the area swept by the blades.

tooltips.name: RadiusFrac
tooltips.title: Blade section radius
tooltips.meaning: How far this propeller section is from the centre, as a fraction of tip radius.
tooltips.effect: It places the section along the blade rather than changing its chord or pitch.
tooltips.example: 0.75 places the section at three quarters of the radius.

tooltips.name: RPM
tooltips.title: Moving propeller RPM
tooltips.meaning: The turning speed of this propeller group in an unsteady analysis.
tooltips.effect: It sets how fast the blades move through the airflow; time-step resolution also needs to be adequate.
tooltips.example: 2,400 RPM corresponds to 40 revolutions per second.

tooltips.name: AlphaStart
tooltips.title: Angle of attack - start
tooltips.meaning: The angle between the aircraft's reference direction and the oncoming airflow. First value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: Changing it changes lift and drag. A real wing can stall at high angles; solver results depend on the chosen stall model.
tooltips.example: Start with a small range of angles rather than assuming a very large angle is valid.

tooltips.name: AlphaEnd
tooltips.title: Angle of attack - end
tooltips.meaning: The angle between the aircraft's reference direction and the oncoming airflow. Last value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: Changing it changes lift and drag. A real wing can stall at high angles; solver results depend on the chosen stall model.
tooltips.example: Start with a small range of angles rather than assuming a very large angle is valid.

tooltips.name: AlphaNpts
tooltips.title: Angle of attack - number of cases
tooltips.meaning: How many evenly spaced values of angle of attack the solver will analyse, including the ends.
tooltips.effect: More values give a finer set of cases and take longer; they do not change the aircraft geometry.
tooltips.example: For one operating point, use 1. With 3 points, 0 to 10 becomes 0, 5 and 10.

tooltips.name: BetaStart
tooltips.title: Sideslip angle - start
tooltips.meaning: The sideways angle between the aircraft's reference direction and the oncoming airflow. First value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: It changes side force and yawing and rolling moments.
tooltips.example: Beta 0 means no sideslip, not no angle of attack.

tooltips.name: BetaEnd
tooltips.title: Sideslip angle - end
tooltips.meaning: The sideways angle between the aircraft's reference direction and the oncoming airflow. Last value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: It changes side force and yawing and rolling moments.
tooltips.example: Beta 0 means no sideslip, not no angle of attack.

tooltips.name: BetaNpts
tooltips.title: Sideslip angle - number of cases
tooltips.meaning: How many evenly spaced values of sideslip angle the solver will analyse, including the ends.
tooltips.effect: More values give a finer set of cases and take longer; they do not change the aircraft geometry.
tooltips.example: For one operating point, use 1. With 3 points, 0 to 10 becomes 0, 5 and 10.

tooltips.name: MachStart
tooltips.title: Mach number - start
tooltips.meaning: Airspeed divided by the local speed of sound. First value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: It describes how compressibility affects airflow; the same Mach need not mean the same speed at every temperature.
tooltips.example: Mach 0.2 means one fifth of the local speed of sound.

tooltips.name: MachEnd
tooltips.title: Mach number - end
tooltips.meaning: Airspeed divided by the local speed of sound. Last value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: It describes how compressibility affects airflow; the same Mach need not mean the same speed at every temperature.
tooltips.example: Mach 0.2 means one fifth of the local speed of sound.

tooltips.name: MachNpts
tooltips.title: Mach number - number of cases
tooltips.meaning: How many evenly spaced values of mach number the solver will analyse, including the ends.
tooltips.effect: More values give a finer set of cases and take longer; they do not change the aircraft geometry.
tooltips.example: For one operating point, use 1. With 3 points, 0 to 10 becomes 0, 5 and 10.

tooltips.name: ReCref
tooltips.title: Reynolds number - start
tooltips.meaning: A number comparing air motion with viscosity, using the reference chord as the length. First value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: It affects skin friction and airfoil behaviour. Very small aircraft can behave differently from scaled-up ones.
tooltips.example: A small model and a full-size aircraft at the same speed need not have the same Reynolds number.

tooltips.name: ReCrefEnd
tooltips.title: Reynolds number - end
tooltips.meaning: A number comparing air motion with viscosity, using the reference chord as the length. Last value in the analysis range.
tooltips.effect: It affects skin friction and airfoil behaviour. Very small aircraft can behave differently from scaled-up ones.
tooltips.example: A small model and a full-size aircraft at the same speed need not have the same Reynolds number.

tooltips.name: ReCrefNpts
tooltips.title: Reynolds number - number of cases
tooltips.meaning: How many evenly spaced values of reynolds number the solver will analyse, including the ends.
tooltips.effect: More values give a finer set of cases and take longer; they do not change the aircraft geometry.
tooltips.example: For one operating point, use 1. With 3 points, 0 to 10 becomes 0, 5 and 10.

tooltips.name: Sref
tooltips.title: Reference wing area
tooltips.meaning: The area used to turn lift and drag forces into comparison numbers called coefficients.
tooltips.effect: Changing this reference rescales the coefficients; it does not add physical wing area.
tooltips.example: Use the same reference area when comparing two sets of CL and CD results.

tooltips.name: Vinf
tooltips.title: Airspeed
tooltips.meaning: The speed of the undisturbed air relative to the aircraft.
tooltips.effect: Airspeed changes aerodynamic forces and propeller operating conditions. It is not the aircraft's speed over the ground.
tooltips.example: A headwind can make airspeed different from ground speed.
tooltips.units: Length per second, consistent with the solver density and geometry inputs.

tooltips.name: Sref
tooltips.title: Reference wing area
tooltips.meaning: The area used to turn lift and drag forces into comparison numbers called coefficients.
tooltips.effect: Changing this reference rescales the coefficients; it does not add physical wing area.
tooltips.example: Use the same reference area when comparing two sets of CL and CD results.

tooltips.name: Vinf
tooltips.title: Airspeed
tooltips.meaning: The speed of the undisturbed air relative to the aircraft.
tooltips.effect: Airspeed changes aerodynamic forces and propeller operating conditions. It is not the aircraft's speed over the ground.
tooltips.example: A headwind can make airspeed different from ground speed.

tooltips.name: bref
tooltips.title: Reference span
tooltips.meaning: The span used to scale rolling and yawing moment coefficients.
tooltips.effect: This is an analysis reference length, not a command to resize the aircraft.
tooltips.example: Keep reference lengths unchanged when comparing coefficients between runs.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: cref
tooltips.title: Reference chord
tooltips.meaning: The chord used to scale pitching moment coefficients.
tooltips.effect: This is an analysis reference length, not a command to resize the aircraft.
tooltips.example: Keep reference lengths unchanged when comparing coefficients between runs.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Rho
tooltips.title: Air density
tooltips.meaning: How much air mass occupies a unit of volume at the flight condition.
tooltips.effect: At the same true airspeed, thinner air gives smaller aerodynamic forces for unchanged coefficients. It also changes propeller loading.
tooltips.example: Air is usually thinner at high altitude. This is not the density of the wing material.
tooltips.units: Mass per length cubed, consistent with geometry and speed: kg/m^3 in SI or slug/ft^3 in slug-ft-s inputs.

tooltips.name: NCPU
tooltips.title: Solver processors
tooltips.meaning: How many processor workers the aerodynamic solver may use.
tooltips.effect: More workers can reduce calculation time on a suitable computer; they do not make the physics more accurate.
tooltips.example: Leave processing capacity for other programs if your PC becomes unresponsive.

tooltips.name: WakeNumIter
tooltips.title: Wake iterations
tooltips.meaning: How many repeated updates are allowed for the airflow trailing behind the aircraft.
tooltips.effect: Enough updates help the result settle. Too few can leave an unconverged answer.
tooltips.example: Compare force histories instead of trusting a result only because the solver finished.

tooltips.name: RootWakeNodes
tooltips.title: Wake nodes
tooltips.meaning: The number of divisions used to describe the trailing airflow.
tooltips.effect: More divisions resolve more wake detail but increase computation.
tooltips.example: Check that adding detail no longer changes the result significantly.

tooltips.name: CLMax2D
tooltips.title: Airfoil maximum lift coefficient
tooltips.meaning: The assumed maximum section lift coefficient used by the selected stall model.
tooltips.effect: It limits the modelled section lift when that model is enabled. It is not automatically the complete wing CLmax.
tooltips.example: Use appropriate airfoil data rather than increasing the number until a design appears to fly.

tooltips.name: StallModel
tooltips.title: Stall model
tooltips.meaning: Choose whether to apply the available approximate stall treatment.
tooltips.effect: This changes the aerodynamic model; it does not make a high-angle result a validated stall prediction.
tooltips.example: A successful solver run is not proof that a real aircraft can fly safely at that angle.

tooltips.name: Symmetry
tooltips.title: Solver mirror symmetry
tooltips.meaning: Solve a symmetric case using the XZ centre plane.
tooltips.effect: It can reduce work, but is only appropriate when the geometry and flight condition support that symmetry.
tooltips.example: A sideslip case or asymmetric aircraft may need a full-model analysis.

tooltips.name: Xcg
tooltips.title: X moment reference
tooltips.meaning: The X coordinate of the point about which aerodynamic moments are reported.
tooltips.effect: Moving the reference point changes reported moments without changing the aircraft shape.
tooltips.example: Use the calculated CG when you want moments about the mass balance point.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Ycg
tooltips.title: Y moment reference
tooltips.meaning: The Y coordinate of the point about which aerodynamic moments are reported.
tooltips.effect: Moving the reference point changes reported moments without changing the aircraft shape.
tooltips.example: Use the calculated CG when you want moments about the mass balance point.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Zcg
tooltips.title: Z moment reference
tooltips.meaning: The Z coordinate of the point about which aerodynamic moments are reported.
tooltips.effect: Moving the reference point changes reported moments without changing the aircraft shape.
tooltips.example: Use the calculated CG when you want moments about the mass balance point.
tooltips.units: Your model length units; use one consistent unit system.

tooltips.name: Density
tooltips.title: Air density
tooltips.meaning: How much air mass occupies a unit of volume at the selected flight condition.
tooltips.effect: It affects aerodynamic forces and Reynolds number, not the mass of the aircraft structure.
tooltips.example: At the same true airspeed, high-altitude air usually produces less lift for the same wing angle.

tooltips.name: Alt
tooltips.title: Flight altitude
tooltips.meaning: Height above sea level used to calculate the atmosphere for this drag estimate.
tooltips.effect: It changes air density, temperature and viscosity. It is not a calculated maximum flight altitude.
tooltips.example: Entering 3,000 m asks for drag at that altitude; it does not prove the aircraft can reach it.

tooltips.name: Mach
tooltips.title: Mach number
tooltips.meaning: Airspeed divided by the local speed of sound.
tooltips.effect: It affects compressibility corrections in the drag estimate.
tooltips.example: Mach 0.2 is one fifth of the local speed of sound.

tooltips.name: Temp
tooltips.title: Air temperature
tooltips.meaning: The temperature of the surrounding air at the flight condition.
tooltips.effect: It affects density, viscosity and the local speed of sound.
tooltips.example: A hot day changes performance even at the same airport elevation.

tooltips.name: DeltaTemp
tooltips.title: Temperature offset
tooltips.meaning: How much warmer or colder the air is than the standard atmosphere at this altitude.
tooltips.effect: It changes the atmosphere estimate without changing altitude.
tooltips.example: An offset of +10 means ten degrees warmer than standard.

tooltips.name: Pres
tooltips.title: Air pressure
tooltips.meaning: The surrounding atmospheric pressure at the flight condition.
tooltips.effect: Pressure together with temperature determines air density in the atmosphere model.
tooltips.example: Air pressure normally falls as you climb.

tooltips.name: DynaVisc
tooltips.title: Air viscosity
tooltips.meaning: How strongly air resists being sheared, or sliding in layers.
tooltips.effect: Viscosity helps determine skin friction and Reynolds number.
tooltips.example: It matters even though air seems much less sticky than oil.

tooltips.name: Re_L
tooltips.title: Reynolds number per unit length
tooltips.meaning: Reynolds number divided by the reference length.
tooltips.effect: Multiplying it by a component length gives that component's Reynolds number, using consistent length units.
tooltips.example: Do not paste a full chord Reynolds number into a per-unit-length field.

tooltips.name: LengthUnit
tooltips.title: Geometry length units
tooltips.meaning: Tell the drag tool what one unit in your geometry represents.
tooltips.effect: Using the wrong units changes physical size and Reynolds number. It does not automatically resize your saved geometry.
tooltips.example: If the model was drawn in metres, choose metres here.

tooltips.name: VinfUnitType
tooltips.title: Airspeed units
tooltips.meaning: Choose how the entered airspeed is measured.
tooltips.effect: A number in knots means a different speed from the same number in metres per second.
tooltips.example: Check the unit before copying a speed from a flight specification.

tooltips.name: FreestreamType
tooltips.title: Atmosphere input method
tooltips.meaning: Choose which information defines the air, such as a standard atmosphere at an altitude.
tooltips.effect: This controls which atmosphere fields are calculated and which you enter yourself.
tooltips.example: Use a standard-atmosphere mode when you know altitude rather than pressure and density.

tooltips.name: ExcresVal
tooltips.title: Extra drag allowance
tooltips.meaning: An allowance for drag from details not represented by the smooth model.
tooltips.effect: The selected allowance type determines whether the number means a percentage, drag count, or drag area.
tooltips.example: Protruding antennas and small gaps can create drag not captured by a simple fuselage.
tooltips.units: Depends on the selected allowance type.

tooltips.name: PercLam
tooltips.title: Laminar-flow percentage
tooltips.meaning: The estimated percentage of surface length with smooth, layered airflow before it becomes turbulent.
tooltips.effect: More laminar flow generally lowers estimated skin-friction drag, but roughness and flight condition can prevent it.
tooltips.example: 50 means 50 percent, not a fraction of 0.5.

tooltips.name: FFUser
tooltips.title: Shape drag factor
tooltips.meaning: A manual factor allowing for extra drag caused by component shape.
tooltips.effect: A larger factor increases the empirical drag estimate; it does not change the physical shape.
tooltips.example: Use a defensible correlation rather than reducing the factor to improve a result.

tooltips.name: Roughness
tooltips.title: Surface roughness
tooltips.meaning: A measure of small bumps on the surface used by applicable drag correlations.
tooltips.effect: A rough surface can alter transition and increase skin-friction drag.
tooltips.example: Rivet heads, dirt and poor finish can matter even on a smooth-looking CAD model.
tooltips.units: Check the selected drag correlation and its roughness units.

lessons.title: The four forces
lessons.summary: What keeps an aircraft moving and supported?
lessons.meaning: Lift and weight act roughly up and down in straight, level flight. Thrust pushes forward; drag resists the motion through air.
lessons.effect: To keep a steady speed and height in this simple case, lift balances weight and thrust balances drag. An imbalance changes motion.
lessons.example: If forward thrust is 1,200 N and drag is 1,000 N, 200 N remains to accelerate the aircraft.
lessons.try_it: Hover over Thrust in the VSPAERO Disk controls. Read its meaning, effect and example.
lessons.caution: The picture describes straight, level flight. Forces tilt during turns and climbs; this is not a complete flight simulator.
lessons.keywords: lift weight thrust drag balance force newton

lessons.title: Thrust and power
lessons.summary: Push is not the same thing as energy per second.
lessons.meaning: Thrust is the pushing or pulling force from a propeller or jet. Power is how quickly an engine or motor supplies energy.
lessons.effect: Extra forward thrust can help you accelerate or climb. How much thrust a propeller makes depends on its blades, RPM, air density and flight speed.
lessons.example: An engine with more power does not automatically produce proportionally more thrust. The propeller must use that power at the required speed.
lessons.try_it: Open Analysis > Aero > VSPAERO, then Disk. Hover over Thrust, Power, RPM and Efficiency before changing an input.
lessons.caution: Entering a thrust value describes an assumed operating point. It does not prove a real engine can deliver it.
lessons.keywords: engine propulsion motor horsepower watts propeller rotor

lessons.title: Lift, angle and stall
lessons.summary: Why raising the nose does not always make more lift.
lessons.meaning: Angle of attack is the angle between a wing reference line and the air arriving at it. Lift is the aerodynamic force perpendicular to that airflow.
lessons.effect: Increasing angle usually increases lift at first. Beyond the real wing's stall angle, separated airflow can reduce lift and control authority.
lessons.example: An aircraft can have a high angle of attack with its nose almost level if its flight path is descending.
lessons.try_it: In VSPAERO, start with a small Alpha range. Compare CL and drag, and check the selected stall treatment.
lessons.caution: Do not treat a linear lift curve at large angles as proof that the wing cannot stall.
lessons.keywords: alpha CL maximum lift CLmax stall airfoil pitch

lessons.title: Drag
lessons.summary: The air resistance your engine must overcome.
lessons.meaning: Drag acts opposite the motion through air. Skin friction and shape cause parasite drag; producing lift also causes induced drag.
lessons.effect: At fixed shape and coefficients, doubling true airspeed makes aerodynamic forces four times larger. The coefficients themselves may also change.
lessons.example: A larger wing may help slow flight but increase skin area. A longer span can reduce lift-related drag at the same lift and speed.
lessons.try_it: Use Parasite Drag for a smooth-body estimate. Use VSPAERO for lift-related effects; understand the method before combining results.
lessons.caution: Do not add results blindly: overlap between drag methods can double-count some contributions.
lessons.keywords: CD CD0 induced parasite friction resistance

lessons.title: Span, area and aspect ratio
lessons.summary: Three different ways to describe a wing.
lessons.meaning: Span is tip-to-tip wing width. For a flat wing, area is the outline's size seen from above. Aspect ratio describes how long and narrow it is: span squared divided by area.
lessons.effect: More area can lower stall speed for the same weight and maximum lift coefficient. More span generally reduces lift-related drag, but adds structural demands.
lessons.example: A rectangular wing with 10 m span and 1.5 m chord has 15 square metres of area and an aspect ratio of about 6.7.
lessons.try_it: Select a Wing and compare Plan totals with Sect values. A section is not necessarily the complete mirrored wing.
lessons.caution: These are geometry values, not guarantees of flight performance. Check units, symmetry and mass.
lessons.keywords: TotalSpan TotalArea TotalAR wing loading mirrored root tip

lessons.title: Chord and taper
lessons.summary: Front to back is not the same as thickness.
lessons.meaning: Chord is the straight-line distance from the wing's front edge to its back edge. Taper is tip chord divided by root chord.
lessons.effect: Changing chord changes wing area. Reducing the tip chord makes a narrower tip; stall behaviour still depends on airfoil shape and twist.
lessons.example: A 2 m root chord and a 1 m tip chord give a taper ratio of 0.5. A taper of 1 means equal chords.
lessons.try_it: On the Wing Sect tab, hover over Root Chord, Tip Chord and Taper. Change one allowed input and watch the calculated values.
lessons.caution: Only certain combinations are independent. A greyed-out geometry value may be calculated from the selected drivers.
lessons.keywords: root tip Avg_Chord driver span

lessons.title: Sweep
lessons.summary: Why some wings lean backward.
lessons.meaning: Sweep is the backward or forward angle of a wing measurement line when viewed from above.
lessons.effect: Sweep can help at high speed by changing compressibility effects, but it has low-speed and structural trade-offs. It is not a universal speed upgrade.
lessons.example: Leading-edge sweep and quarter-chord sweep are different measurements on a tapered wing.
lessons.try_it: In Wing > Sect, check Sweep Location before comparing angles. 0 is the leading edge; 0.25 is quarter-chord.
lessons.caution: An unswept quarter-chord line can still have swept-looking leading and trailing edges.
lessons.keywords: Sweep_Location Sec_Sweep leading edge quarter chord

lessons.title: Dihedral and twist
lessons.summary: Two different kinds of wing angle.
lessons.meaning: Dihedral is the wing's upward tilt seen from the front. Twist changes the airfoil angle as you move along the wing.
lessons.effect: Dihedral affects response to sideslip. Tip washout means a lower tip angle and can help the root stall before the tips, depending on the whole design.
lessons.example: A shallow V seen head-on is dihedral. A tip angled 2 degrees below the root has 2 degrees of washout.
lessons.try_it: Change these separately on the Wing Sect tab and inspect the model from the front and side.
lessons.caution: Positive dihedral is not a promise that the aircraft will level itself. Stability depends on the complete aircraft.
lessons.keywords: roll sideslip stability washout Twist relative absolute

lessons.title: Airfoil, camber and thickness
lessons.summary: The shape of one slice through a wing.
lessons.meaning: An airfoil is the wing cross-section. Camber is the bend of its middle line. Thickness ratio is maximum thickness divided by chord.
lessons.effect: These change lift, drag, pitching behaviour and room for structure. Chord and thickness are separate dimensions.
lessons.example: With a 1 m chord and thickness ratio 0.12, maximum thickness is about 0.12 m. Camber 0.02 means 2 percent of chord.
lessons.try_it: Open a Wing's Airfoil tab. Compare the shape before and after a small thickness or camber change.
lessons.caution: The drawn shape alone does not tell you its maximum lift or stall characteristics. Use appropriate aerodynamic data.
lessons.keywords: NACA ThickChord CamberLoc Chord CLmax

lessons.title: Mass and centre of gravity
lessons.summary: Where the aircraft balances matters as much as its size.
lessons.meaning: Mass is how much matter the aircraft contains. Weight is the gravity force acting on it. Centre of gravity, or CG, is its mass balance point.
lessons.effect: Moving a heavy part shifts the CG. Whether the aircraft can be trimmed and remain stable depends on aerodynamic forces and moments too.
lessons.example: A 10 kg battery moved rearward shifts the CG rearward; the amount depends on the other masses and their positions.
lessons.try_it: Set meaningful mass assumptions on component Mass tabs, then run Analysis > Mass Prop and enable Draw Cg.
lessons.caution: A visible CG marker is not a safe CG envelope. QASP has not certified a stable or controllable aircraft.
lessons.keywords: weight density battery balance trim stability inertia

lessons.title: Units and model size
lessons.summary: A number such as 10 does not automatically mean metres.
lessons.meaning: Geometry uses numerical length units. Analysis and export tools need a consistent interpretation such as metres or feet.
lessons.effect: A unit mismatch can make the same model look plausible while giving incorrect size, Reynolds number, mass or forces.
lessons.example: If a fuselage length of 7 means 7 metres, use metres consistently where the analysis asks for geometry units.
lessons.try_it: Write your chosen length and mass units in your project notes. Check each analysis's unit selections before running it.
lessons.caution: Do not assume changing a unit selector rescales existing geometry. Check what that particular control does.
lessons.keywords: metres meters feet SI imperial conversion scale

lessons.title: Position and rotation
lessons.summary: Move a part without accidentally resizing it.
lessons.meaning: X, Y and Z are the model's coordinate directions. Position moves a component; rotation turns it. Relative coordinates refer to its parent.
lessons.effect: Moving a wing or tail changes aircraft layout and can change balance and aerodynamic moments. It does not automatically resize the part.
lessons.example: To make a single vertical fin, rotate a Wing about X on XForm and disable the mirror that would overlap it.
lessons.try_it: Use the XForm inputs for accurate placement. View > Fit All On Screen brings the model back into view.
lessons.caution: Do not rely on dragging in the 3D view to move geometry; view rotation and component placement are different actions.
lessons.keywords: XForm X_Rotation Y Z translate attach parent

lessons.title: 1. Start with the body
lessons.summary: A shape exercise, not a flight-ready aircraft.
lessons.meaning: A fuselage is the main body. QASP builds it from a series of cross-sections, like slices through a loaf.
lessons.effect: The section sizes and positions determine space for payload and the exterior shape. A longer body does not automatically assign more real mass.
lessons.example: For practice, choose metres and sketch a body about 7 m long. This example size is not a recommendation for a real aircraft.
lessons.try_it: File > New. Open Model > Geometry, choose Fuselage, and press Add. In its Design tab, set Length; inspect section widths and heights.
lessons.caution: Save often as .vsp3. Undo Parameter Change reverses supported parameter edits, not every modelling action.
lessons.keywords: first aircraft tutorial fuselage beginner new add

lessons.title: 2. Add and size a wing
lessons.summary: Choose independent inputs, then inspect the totals.
lessons.meaning: A Wing component can represent a main wing, tail or fin. Its Sect tab describes individual sections; Plan shows totals.
lessons.effect: The selected drivers are the values you control. The remaining shape values are calculated so the section stays consistent.
lessons.example: For a practice rectangular wing, use section span 5, root chord 1.5 and tip chord 1.5. XZ symmetry gives about 10 total span and 15 area.
lessons.try_it: Choose Wing in Model > Geometry and press Add. On Sect, select Span, Root Chord and Tip Chord as drivers. Set sweep to 0 and enter the example values.
lessons.caution: Check Plan totals and symmetry rather than assuming section values describe the whole aircraft. This is only a geometry example.
lessons.keywords: tutorial drivers rectangular Area Aspect 10 15

lessons.title: 3. Add tails and save
lessons.summary: Use the same Wing tool for different lifting surfaces.
lessons.meaning: A horizontal tail helps control nose-up and nose-down motion. A vertical fin helps control nose-left and nose-right motion.
lessons.effect: Tail size and distance from the CG affect available control moments. Tail volume, trim and stability need proper analysis.
lessons.example: Add a smaller Wing behind the main wing as a horizontal tail. Add a separate Wing rotated about X for a fin.
lessons.try_it: Position parts with XForm. Turn off XZ symmetry for a single fin on the centreline. Use File > Save As and keep the .vsp3 model.
lessons.caution: Adding tails does not prove the aircraft is stable. This lesson deliberately gives no supposedly safe tail size.
lessons.keywords: tutorial horizontal vertical fin rudder elevator tailplane save

lessons.title: CompGeom: shape checks
lessons.summary: A geometry check, not a flight test.
lessons.meaning: CompGeom intersects component surfaces and reports geometric quantities such as areas and volumes.
lessons.effect: It can help identify problems with the model and supplies useful geometric information. It does not calculate a maximum speed or altitude.
lessons.example: If two components overlap unexpectedly, their exposed areas and volumes may not match a simple sum of the separate shapes.
lessons.try_it: Open Analysis > CompGeom. Choose the intended geometry set, compute, and inspect the messages and output.
lessons.caution: It is not a mandatory first step for every other analysis. Each tool has its own geometry preparation and assumptions.
lessons.keywords: mesh intersection wetted area volume compute

lessons.title: Mass Prop: calculate balance
lessons.summary: Give the tool mass assumptions first.
lessons.meaning: Mass Properties estimates total mass, CG and resistance to rotation, called inertia, from the included geometry and mass inputs.
lessons.effect: The result depends on your material density, shell mass, point masses and selected sets. It cannot discover the weight of an unmodelled battery.
lessons.example: Model a skin by mass per area, or a solid by mass per volume. Check that you have not counted both unintentionally.
lessons.try_it: Enter component mass assumptions. Open Analysis > Mass Prop, select the intended sets, then Compute and Draw Cg.
lessons.caution: A calculated mass is only as good as the inputs. It is not a weighed aircraft or a validated stability result.
lessons.keywords: density shell inertia Ixx Iyy Izz balance CG

lessons.title: Parasite Drag: estimate drag
lessons.summary: Estimate one important part of the drag budget.
lessons.meaning: Parasite Drag estimates skin-friction and shape-related drag using geometry, atmosphere inputs and empirical equations.
lessons.effect: The result changes with speed, altitude, surface condition and reference area. It does not include every source of real-aircraft drag.
lessons.example: Run the same shape at two speeds or altitudes while keeping unit choices and reference area consistent.
lessons.try_it: Open Analysis > Aero > Parasite Drag. Check geometry length units, airspeed units, atmosphere, reference area and included components.
lessons.caution: This result alone cannot give top speed, climb rate or maximum altitude. Lift-related drag and available propulsion are also needed.
lessons.keywords: CD0 drag counts laminar turbulent friction atmosphere

lessons.title: VSPAERO: airflow and loads
lessons.summary: Ask a specific question at a specific flight condition.
lessons.meaning: VSPAERO estimates aerodynamic forces and moments using a prepared model and chosen flight conditions.
lessons.effect: You can study lift, drag, pressure and stability-related results within the method's assumptions. The solver does not automatically validate a complete aircraft.
lessons.example: An Alpha range of 0 to 8 with 5 cases requests 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 degrees. A real stall prediction needs suitable modelling and validation.
lessons.try_it: Open Analysis > Aero > VSPAERO. Check included geometry, reference quantities, flow conditions and solver messages before trusting a plot.
lessons.caution: Wait for results to converge and check resolution. A completed run can still contain physically unsuitable assumptions.
lessons.keywords: alpha Mach Reynolds CL CD moments convergence solver

lessons.title: Read CL, CD and L/D
lessons.summary: Comparison numbers are not forces by themselves.
lessons.meaning: CL is a lift coefficient. CD is a drag coefficient. They express forces relative to air density, speed and reference area. L/D compares lift with drag.
lessons.effect: A larger L/D means less drag for the same lift at that condition, but says nothing by itself about takeoff safety or engine capability.
lessons.example: If CL is 0.6 and CD is 0.03 using the same references, L/D is 20. To obtain a force, density, speed and reference area are still needed.
lessons.try_it: Check the flight condition and reference area before comparing plots or coefficients from different tools.
lessons.caution: Do not compare L/D across different configurations without understanding what drag contributions each result includes.
lessons.keywords: lift drag polar coefficient efficiency reference area

lessons.title: How high or fast can it fly?
lessons.summary: Know when the available information is not enough.
lessons.meaning: Maximum speed depends on where available thrust balances total drag. Climbing needs excess propulsive capability as well as adequate lift.
lessons.effect: A useful altitude estimate needs aircraft weight, a validated drag and lift model, and engine or motor performance as altitude and speed change.
lessons.example: Typing 5,000 m into an atmosphere input only requests conditions at 5,000 m. It is not a calculated ceiling.
lessons.try_it: Collect consistent mass, aerodynamic and propulsion data before making a performance estimate. The current QASP build has no validated automatic ceiling calculation.
lessons.caution: Do not interpret an atmosphere setting or a successful solver run as a claim that a real aircraft can reach that altitude.
lessons.keywords: ceiling max maximum altitude top speed climb performance thrust power

lessons.title: Meshes and external solvers
lessons.summary: A mesh prepares a calculation; it is not the answer.
lessons.meaning: A mesh divides surfaces into small pieces. CFD Mesh prepares aerodynamic geometry; FEA Structure prepares structural modelling data.
lessons.effect: Resolution, intersections, materials, loads and boundary conditions all affect the later solver results.
lessons.example: More triangles may improve geometric detail, but they cannot fix the wrong load case or missing material data.
lessons.try_it: Use the relevant mesh tool for a defined analysis task and inspect its warnings and exported files.
lessons.caution: Generating a mesh does not calculate structural strength or certify an aircraft. External solving and validation may still be required.
lessons.keywords: CFD FEA structure triangles grid external solver stress

lessons.title: Which other analysis tool?
lessons.summary: Pick a tool by the question it answers.
lessons.meaning: Planar Slice measures cross-sections. Projected Area measures the silhouette from a chosen direction. Geometry Analysis checks geometric relationships.
lessons.effect: DegenGeom creates simplified geometry data. Trimmed Surfaces prepares intersected surfaces. Wave Drag addresses a particular high-speed drag method.
lessons.example: Use Projected Area for a silhouette-area question, not as a substitute for aerodynamic lift or total drag.
lessons.try_it: Open the corresponding Analysis menu item and check its inputs and reference documentation before computing.
lessons.caution: No one tool proves that the aircraft flies. Do not assume every tool must be run in a fixed sequence.
lessons.keywords: planar slice projected area degengeom trimmed surfaces wave drag analysis order
